meta.title: Atlas of Input Representation Methods
meta.classification_unit: One grounded route: a single source object carried through its transformation chain to the model-visible carrier consumed by the model.
meta.organizing_principle: Partition routes by the model-visible carrier mechanism. Biological modality, lifecycle phase, text role, and fusion topology are orthogonal dimensions; they do not decide the family unless they change the carrier that reaches the model.

families.name: Text-native token streams
families.definition: Routes whose visible carrier is ordinary text tokens, including free-form prompts, structured task scaffolds, and serialized biological context rendered as text. The biologic content is carried by language tokens rather than dense vectors, images, or geometric states.
families.structural_criterion: The generative backbone consumes standard text tokens, even when the text is biologically specialized or template-driven.

leaves.name: Plain language prompts and questions
leaves.definition: Natural-language prompts, questions, instructions, or conversational turns that reach the model as ordinary text without a specialized biological serialization step.
include_when: The visible carrier is plain prose, a question, or an instruction.
The route does not require a domain-specific serializer before model intake.
exclude_when: The source is first converted into a gene list, cell sentence, ranked profile, or other biological serialization.
The visible carrier is a dense embedding, an image, or a diffusion state.

leaves.name: Structured biological prompts and task scaffolds
leaves.definition: Text prompts that encode explicit biological slots, metadata fields, retrieval directives, benchmark scaffolds, or relation-context prompts.
include_when: The text contains explicit biological fields, slots, or template-like task structure.
The prompt functions as a structured control frame rather than free-form conversation.
exclude_when: The input is only plain conversational text with no task scaffolding.
The carrier is a biological sentence serialization or a dense embedding prefix.

leaves.name: Serialized biological context and ordered profiles
leaves.definition: Text-token sequences produced by serializing cells, genes, neighborhoods, ranked profiles, or multi-cell contexts into language-like sentences or ordered lists before model intake.
include_when: The route converts biological objects into cell sentences, spatial sentences, gene lists, ranked expression profiles, or comparable serialized text.
The visible carrier is a textual summary of biological context, often across multiple nearby entities or samples.
exclude_when: The route is a simple question or instruction with no biological serialization.
The route is a fixed slot template rather than a serialized biological narrative.
The carrier is a dense vector, image, or diffusion state.

families.name: Discrete biological symbol streams
families.definition: Routes whose biological source is represented as a discrete symbol stream native to or added to the tokenizer, rather than as prose text or dense embeddings. This includes biological BPE streams, multi-track structural alphabets, and learned quantized codebook IDs.
families.structural_criterion: The model-visible carrier is a tokenized biological sequence or structured biological symbol stream.

leaves.name: Native biological token streams
leaves.definition: DNA, RNA, or protein corpora rendered as discrete biological tokens through an extended tokenizer or chunking protocol.
include_when: The route uses tokenized DNA, RNA, protein, or comparable biological sequence corpora.
The visible form is a chunked biological token stream rather than a prose prompt or embedding.
exclude_when: The route is an ordinary text prompt or instruction.
The route is a dense embedding prefix or an image patch input.

leaves.name: Multi-track structural symbol streams
leaves.definition: A token stream that explicitly preserves multiple structural tracks or aligned alphabets, such as sequence plus secondary-structure or tertiary-structure tracks.
include_when: The route preserves several aligned structural tracks in one discrete token stream.
The visible carrier is a structured symbolic alphabet, not an embedding.
exclude_when: The route is a single-track tokenized corpus.
The route is a continuous prefix, image patch, or diffusion state.

leaves.name: Learned quantized IDs and codebook tokens
leaves.definition: Routes whose biological content is rendered as learned discrete IDs from VQ, RVQ, or codebook-style tokenizers. These are discrete symbols, not continuous embeddings and not native tokenizer words.
include_when: The route uses VQ, RVQ, or codebook IDs as model-visible inputs.
The discrete IDs are embedded into the LLM vocabulary or otherwise treated as symbol tokens.
The route is not just a continuous latent prefix.
exclude_when: The route is a continuous embedding or resampler output.
The route is ordinary prose text or a native biological token corpus.

families.name: Dense continuous carriers
families.definition: Routes whose model-visible form is a learned dense vector, soft-token block, prefix embedding, resampled latent, or similar continuous carrier inserted into a generative backbone. The biological source is encoded rather than discretely tokenized.
families.structural_criterion: The source is converted into continuous embeddings, soft tokens, or learned latent blocks before reaching the generator.

leaves.name: Direct projected embeddings
leaves.definition: A continuous embedding projected from a biological encoder into the language or multimodal backbone, typically via a linear layer, projector, or latent-space mapping.
include_when: The route explicitly projects biological inputs into an embedding space or unified latent space.
The visible carrier is a dense vector block rather than text tokens or image patches.
exclude_when: The carrier is a fixed prefix block of learned virtual tokens.
The carrier is an image patch sequence or a discrete biological token stream.
The carrier is a diffusion state or geometric constraint.

leaves.name: Virtual-token prefixes
leaves.definition: A fixed-length block of learned virtual tokens or multimodal prefix tokens that stands in for the biological source before being concatenated or inserted into the backbone.
include_when: The route uses a fixed prefix, placeholder-bearing virtual-token block, or multimodal prefix.
The biological source is not passed as ordinary text but as a learned prefix-like embedding bundle.
exclude_when: The route uses direct projection into a latent space without a dedicated prefix block.
The carrier is a pooled embedding, an image patch set, or a diffusion state.

leaves.name: Connector-mediated embeddings
leaves.definition: A dense carrier that reaches the backbone through a learned connector such as cross-attention, a resampler, a query-former, an adapter layer, or a query connector.
include_when: The route explicitly uses cross-attention, a resampler, a query-former, a query connector, or an adapter.
The biological content is converted to dense tokens before fusion with the backbone.
exclude_when: The route is a fixed virtual-token prefix.
The route is a direct embedding projection without a separate mediator.
The route is a raw image or a discrete biological token stream.

leaves.name: Pooled or aggregated embeddings
leaves.definition: A continuous carrier formed by aggregating multiple inputs into one embedding before model intake, such as averaging selected-cell embeddings or similar pooling operations.
include_when: The route compresses multiple biological items into one embedding before downstream use.
The visible form is a pooled representation rather than a single-source projection.
exclude_when: The route keeps separate tokens for each instance in the prompt.
The route uses raw images, discrete tokens, or a diffusion state.

families.name: Geometric and diffusion-state carriers
families.definition: Routes whose model-visible form is a geometric constraint, coordinate state, or noisy latent state used by a diffusion or structure-generation model. These routes are structurally distinct from ordinary embeddings because the carrier is organized by geometry or diffusion time.
families.structural_criterion: The model-visible carrier is a coordinate, constraint object, or time-indexed noisy latent state rather than a token sequence or patch grid.

leaves.definition: A time-indexed noisy latent state or training state used directly in a diffusion process.

exclude_when: The route is a static coordinate constraint or a text prompt.
The route is an image, token stream, or dense embedding prefix.

leaves.name: Coordinate, backbone, or shape conditioning
leaves.definition: A geometric conditioning route in which the model receives coordinates, backbones, substructures, or point-cloud-derived geometry as the visible carrier.

The model-visible form is geometric rather than textual.
exclude_when: The route is an abstract symbolic label or a free-form text prompt.
The route is a noisy diffusion state rather than a stable geometric condition.

architectures.paper_title: Any-to-Any Learning in Computational Pathology via Triplet Multimodal Pretraining

figure.caption: Figure 1: Overview of our pretraining framework, ALTER . (a) ALTER processes each modality using modality-specific encoders, followed by a universal sequence Transformer and task-specific projection heads for downstream prediction. (b) The three-tiered constraints of ALTER, which can enable model to align multimodal inputs without requiring full modality pairing. (c) ALTER can be applied to any downstream task by integrating task-specific projection heads for fine-tuning.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel model architecture/workflow figure for a biomedical multi-modal foundation model. Panel (a) “Overall Architecture” shows inputs from whole slide images, omics, and pathology reports processed by modality-specific tokenizers/encoders, sequence projectors, a Universal Sequence Transformer, and task-specific projection heads. Panel (b) “Stage 1: Pre-training Universal Sequence Transformer” shows contrastive and masked language modeling objectives across WSI, omics, and text features, including inter-modal, inter-sample, and intra-modal contrast. Panel (c) “Stage 2: Training Task Projection Heads with Downstream Tasks” shows downstream applications including cancer subtyping, survival analysis, and report generation. No quantitative axes or experimental results are shown; the main content is a proposed multimodal training pipeline/architecture.

architectures.paper_title: Aligning LLMs with Biomedical Knowledge using Balanced Fine-Tuning

figure.caption: Figure 6: Workflow for extracting biological embeddings from LLM-BFT. a : LLM-BFT generates profile texts for entities of interest (e.g., a specific gene). The gene profile text is encoded by OpenAI TEXT-EMBEDDING-ADA-002 (the same text encoder GenePT uses) to obtain gene embeddings, so that GenePT (GPT-4o + ada-002) and LLM-BFT (BFT-70B + ada-002) differ only in the LLM that produces the profile text. b : For a single-cell dataset, gene embeddings are weighted by gene expression values to generate cell embeddings.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic with two labeled panels, **a** and **b**. Panel **a** shows an LLM-based gene text embedding pipeline: a user prompt (“Tell me about gene.”) is processed by **LLM-BFT**, producing an LLM response with gene name/function/interaction text; texts for gene x through gene y are converted via **Text to embedding** into a **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix. Panel **b** shows a cell-by-gene expression matrix for **M cells** and **N genes** multiplied by the **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix to produce a **cell embedding (M, 2048)** matrix. Main visible message: gene-level text embeddings are derived from LLM responses and combined with gene expression data to generate cell embeddings.

architectures.paper_title: Bio-BLIP: A Multimodal Architecture for Transferable Reasoning in Genomic Variant Interpretation

figure.caption: Figure 1: (a) Embeddings (E) from Biological Foundation Models (BioFMs) are input to Bio-BLIP to provide multiple modalities of information, here from AlphaGenome , GenePT , and ESM-2 . (b) Modality-specific Q-formers align diverse biological embeddings with captions of genomic variants, which contain functional and locational information. The Q-formers output query tokens encoding relevant information from each modality. (c) The Master Qformer integrates modality-specific tokens through cross-attention, producing a fixed-length visual prefix (d) The LLM, its weights frozen , takes as input the multimodal prefix and a prompt. During pretraining, the LLM loss backpropagates only to train the Q-formers. Pretraining and evaluation is conducted on variant annotation; all weights are frozen and the model is then applied to downstream evaluation tasks.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Model architecture/workflow diagram labeled “BioBLIP Architecture.” It shows panel-like labels A-D: A indicates multiple input embedding sources (AlphaGenome Ref/Alt embeddings, GenoPT embeddings, ESM Protein embeddings) as blue triangular inputs E1, E2, … En; B shows modality-specific query modules (“DNA Qformer,” “Gene Qformer,” “Protein Qformer”) producing DNA/gene/protein-specific query tokens; C shows a “Master Qformer” receiving query tokens plus an instruction describing genomic variant context and outputting a fixed-length variant prefix; D shows this prefix fed with a text prompt into a “Frozen LLM,” producing a generated variant annotation JSON.

No quantitative axes or plots are present. The biological/model content shown is a multimodal genomic variant annotation architecture integrating DNA, gene, and protein embeddings for tasks including variant annotation, target gene identification, and regulatory variant prioritization. Main visible finding/claim: BioBLIP uses chained Q-former modules to convert heterogeneous biological embeddings into an LLM-compatible prefix for structured variant annotation.

figure.caption: Figure 2: The overview of BioMedGPT-10B. BioMedGPT-LM is the large language model of BioMedGPT, which serves as a cognitive core to jointly comprehend various biological modalities through natural language. architectures.paper_title: BIOREASON: Incentivizing Multimodal Biological Reasoning within a DNA-LLM Model

figure.caption: Figure 1: BIOREASON Architecture. Schematic representation of our novel multimodal framework that integrates a DNA foundation model with a Large Language Model.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a genomics-language model system. It shows DNA sequences passed through a frozen Evo2-1B model, then a learnable linear projection aligning Evo2 embeddings to Qwen3 dimensions. These projected DNA embeddings are stacked with tokenized text embeddings from a BioReason chat template and Qwen3 tokenizer, using special DNA pad/start/end tokens and a Qwen3 embedding matrix. The combined embeddings feed into a Qwen3-4B model.

Visible labels include “Stacked DNA and Text Embeddings,” “Frozen Evo2-1B,” “Learnable Linear Projection,” “Qwen3 Tokenizer,” “Qwen3 Embedding Matrix,” “BioReason Chat Template,” “Question,” and “Response (with reasoning).” The example biomedical prompt concerns chromosome 12, pathway definition involving LRRK2, CYCS, APAF1, CASP9, and CASP3, and asks about the biological effect of an LRRK2 allele. The response panel gives chain-of-thought-style tags and concludes “Parkinson’s disease.”

Main visible point: the figure illustrates a multimodal architecture combining DNA sequence embeddings with biomedical text prompts to generate disease-related reasoning responses.

figure.visible_model_interface: Frozen Evo2-1B, learnable linear projection, Qwen3 tokenizer, Qwen3 embedding matrix, and BioReason chat template with special DNA tokens.

architectures.paper_title: BIOVERSE: Representation Alignment of Biomedical Modalities to LLMs for Multi-Modal Reasoning

figure.caption: Figure 1: BIOVERSE base architecture: a modality-specific BioFM encodes a biological entity, and its output embeddings are mapped by a projection layer into the LLM's embedding space via special tokens (e.g. [BIO] ). In the alignment stage, only the projection layer P θ is trainable, while the encoder f b and the LLM g remain frozen. In the subsequent instruction-tuning stage, we allow both P θ and the low-rank adapter (LORA) within the LLM to be trainable. Stage 1 (S1) can be trained using autoregressive (AR) or contrastive (CT) loss, while stage 2 (S2) is always AR.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Figure type: workflow/model architecture diagram for a biomedical machine learning method integrating scRNA-seq data and text prompts/labels.

Visible panels/labels: Inputs on the left include “scRNA-seq Data” with a heatmap-like expression matrix labeled row = cell, column = gene, color = expression value, plus “Text (Prompt)” and “Text (Label)” examples. The center shows BioEncoder, LLM Tokenizer, LLM Embedding Layer, CLS/X-pooling, projection layers, and a 2-layer MLP. The right side shows a LoRA module and “LLM Forward Pass,” with training paths labeled S1 and S2. Colored annotations indicate BIO token injection, CT training, and AR auto-regressive training.

Quantity/process shown: It depicts how cell embeddings from scRNA-seq are projected into the LLM token space and injected as soft tokens alongside prompt embeddings, then used to predict label tokens such as a cell type.

Main visible finding/message: The diagram presents a model pipeline for cell-type prediction or annotation using scRNA-seq-derived embeddings combined with LLM prompt/label token embeddings, with optional LoRA fine-tuning and auto-regressive training.

architectures.paper_title: Scaling Large Language Models for Next-Generation Single-Cell Analysis.

figure.caption: Figure 1: C2S-Scale unifies transcriptomics and natural language for scalable single-cell analysis. A , The C2S-Scale corpus integrates over 50 million single-cell transcriptomes curated from the CELLxGENE and Human Cell Atlas repositories, linking transcriptomic profiles with rich cell, tissue, and donor-level metadata as well as scientific abstracts and papers. B , C2S-Scale expands upon the Cell2Sentence framework by increasing model capacity up to 27 billion parameters, building a multi-task training corpus of over 1 trillion tokens, and expanding task diversity to include multimodal and multicellular inputs. C , Transcriptomic profiles are transformed into 'cell sentences', ordered sequences of gene names ranked by expression level. This enables the direct application of pretrained LLMs without requiring architectural modifications. D , C2S-Scale is initialized from pre-trained LLM checkpoints. An initial training phase on cell sentences is followed by instruction fine-tuning for a variety of downstream tasks. E , This unified training regime enables broad downstream capabilities, ranging from standard cell annotation to complex tasks like perturbation prediction and biological question answering.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel schematic overview figure for a biomedical AI model/workflow, likely a cell-language foundation model.

Figure type: conceptual workflow/model architecture diagram with labeled panels A-E.

Visible panels and labels:
- A. Data Sources and Annotations: icons for single-cell data, cell clusters, tissue sections, paper abstracts, and donor metadata. Reported scale includes 800+ datasets, 170M+ single-cell and bulk samples, 100M+ annotations, 21M+ perturbations, and 1B+ tokens.
- B. Scaling Dimensions: four boxed concepts: Model Capacity, Dataset Size, Multimodality, and Context Diversity.
- C. Cell Sentence Representation: converts a gene expression matrix with cells and genes into “cell sentences” listing gene tokens.
- D. Model Training Procedure: three-stage training flow: natural language pre-training with a base LLM, continued training on cell sentences to create C2S-Scale, then instruction fine-tuning for downstream tasks.
- E. Downstream Tasks: examples include cell type annotation, cell generation, perturbation response prediction, cluster captioning, dataset interpretation, and question answering.

Biological/model quantity shown: scale and modality of single-cell datasets, gene-expression-derived token sequences, and model training/use cases.

Main visible finding/message: the figure presents a unified framework for training a language-model-based system on large-scale single-cell, perturbation, metadata, and text resources, enabling multiple downstream biological interpretation and generation tasks.

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical experimental figure showing a virtual drug-screening workflow and validation results.

Panel A is a schematic workflow labeled “Virtual Screening Workflow”: primary tumors with immune context-positive profiles and immune-neutral cell lines are screened against a compound library of 4000+ drugs using C2S, identifying hits that increase MHC-I antigen presentation gene set score versus compounds with no effect.

Panel B is a volcano/scatter plot titled “Primary Tumor Screen Results,” with x-axis “Predicted Antigen Presentation Score” and y-axis “-log10(p-value).” Points are categorized by legend as Reported, Plausible, Novel, and star-marked “Silmitasertib.” A zoomed inset highlights drugs including crizotinib, nutlin-3, GSK-126, trametinib, afatinib, paclitaxel, and silmitasertib, with “16 / 23 Reported or Plausible.”

Panel C is a bar plot for “Trametinib + IFNβ (Known Hit - Positive Control)” measuring “HLA ABC MFI” across trametinib concentrations in nM, comparing DMSO only versus DMSO + 5 U/ml IFNβ. HLA ABC MFI increases with treatment, especially with IFNβ.

Panel D is a bar plot titled “Silmitasertib Context Specificity,” showing predicted antigen presentation score higher in “Primary Tumor Context” than “WAGA Cell Line Context,” marked significant.

Panel E is a bar plot for “Silmitasertib + IFNβ (Novel Hit - C2S-predicted)” measuring “HLA ABC MFI” across silmitasertib concentrations in nM, comparing DMSO only versus DMSO + 2 U/ml IFNβ. The main visible finding is that silmitasertib with IFNβ strongly increases HLA ABC MFI relative to DMSO-only conditions.

architectures.paper_title: CaLMFlow: Volterra Flow Matching using Causal Language Models

figure.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the CaLMFlow framework. CaLMFlow takes as input textual conditions and flows and generates the next time point for the flows. The textual condition is tokenized and embedded using the LLM tokenizer and embedding layer while the conditional flows are transformed into spatial-temporal tokens using a learned projection. If multiple conditional flows are input simultaneously, the tokens are ordered by flow, space, and then time. The LLM applies causal language modeling and generates the next time point for each flow.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for generating conditional single-cell flows. The figure has four main panels labeled “Input Conditional Flows,” “Tokenized Flow Tensor,” “Next Token Prediction,” and “Generated Flows.” It shows source distributions at `t=0` conditioned on text labels such as cell type and image labels, mapped into a tokenized tensor over time/flow, cell state, and trajectories. The sequentialized tokens are passed to an LLM for next-token prediction using a Volterra integral equation formulation, then decoded with a VAE decoder to produce generated flow distributions at times `t=0`, `t=0.1`, `t=0.2`, …, `t=1`. The main visible idea is a conditional generative pipeline that learns and extrapolates temporal flow trajectories from multimodal conditions.

figure.visible_model_interface: Tokenized flow tensor feeding the LLM next-token prediction path.

architectures.paper_title: Cell2Text: Multimodal LLM for Generating Single-Cell Descriptions from RNA-Seq Data

figure.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Cell2Text framework. The model takes single-cell RNA-seq profiles as input and processes them through a pretrained Geneformer encoder to generate contextualized gene-level embeddings. These embeddings are projected into the semantic space of the language model via a lightweight adapter module, aligning biological signals with linguistic representations. A pretrained, instruction-tuned LLM decoder then generates structured natural language descriptions that capture cellular identity, tissue of origin, disease associations, and pathway activity.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Model architecture/workflow diagram for generating or modeling single-cell descriptions from gene expression and metadata. It shows a cell with genes `Gene Z`, `Gene E`, ..., `Gene C` passed through a “cell encoder” to produce gene embeddings, then a “modality adapter” projecting dimensions labeled `+512`, `2048`, `3072`. These embeddings are combined with instruction embeddings and prompt embeddings as input to a language model decoder.

Left side lists cell metadata such as cell type, developmental stage, disease, sex, tissue, and pathway annotations, which form a textual cell description `Cp`. Bottom right shows next-token probability `p`, with the training objective labeled `Lsft = LCrossEntropy(Cp, p)`. Main visible point: the figure illustrates a supervised fine-tuning pipeline aligning single-cell gene/modal embeddings with text generation through a language model decoder.

architectures.paper_title: Cell2Text: Multimodal LLM for generating textual descriptions from single-cell RNA-Seq profiles

figure.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the Cell2Text framework. The model takes single-cell RNA-seq profiles as input and processes them through a pretrained Geneformer encoder to generate contextualized gene-level embeddings. These embeddings are projected into the semantic space of the language model via a lightweight adapter module, aligning biological signals with linguistic representations. A pretrained, instruction-tuned LLM decoder then generates structured natural language descriptions that capture cellular identity, tissue of origin, disease associations, and pathway activity.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Figure type: schematic workflow/model architecture diagram.

Visible labels/panels: The diagram shows a single-cell input sequence labeled “cell 1: Gene Z Gene E ... Gene C,” passed through a “cell encoder” to “gene embeddings,” then through a “modality adapter.” It also shows “Cells Metadata” including cell type, developmental stage, disease, sex, tissue, and pathway terms. These metadata are converted into a natural-language “cell description (Cp).” The lower section shows concatenated “instruction embeddings,” “gene embeddings,” and “prompt embeddings” feeding a “language model decoder,” which outputs “next token probability p.” A loss is shown as cross-entropy, approximately `Lsft = LCrossEntropy(Cp, p)`.

Biological/model quantity shown: Integration of single-cell gene expression embeddings and metadata-derived text prompts into a language-model decoder for supervised fine-tuning or cell-description generation.

Main visible finding/message: The architecture maps single-cell gene information and metadata into embeddings, aligns them through an adapter, and trains a language model to generate a textual cell description using next-token prediction loss.

figure.caption: Fig. 1  |  CellHermes  construction  by  integrating  different  self-supervised  learning techniques. a.  Comparative diagram of different foundation model construction between traditional  methods  and  our  method; In traditional methods, we usually take one of the
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure for a biomedical AI paper. Panels are labeled **a–d**.

- **Panel a:** Compares two strategies: training a foundation model from scratch from single-omics data using tokenization, LLM architecture, and pretraining, versus fine-tuning existing NLP LLMs for CellHermes using multiple omics data, textualization, and fine-tuning.
- **Panel b:** Shows emulation of self-supervised learning with question-answer prompts. Includes gene expression data converted into masked cell sequences for **MLM in sequence** and **autoregressive sequence** tasks, plus a protein-protein network used for **mask node prediction in graph** and **mask link prediction in graph**. Reconstructed cells/graphs are shown on the right.
- **Panel c:** Shows human-AI collaboration for prompt design, creating AI-generated diverse prompts from human-written prompts, then CellHermes training via instruction datasets and open-source LLMs such as Llama, Qwen, and DeepSeek with LoRA instruction fine-tuning.
- **Panel d:** Shows CellHermes applications as an encoder, predictor, and explainer. Inputs include gene/cell text prompts, embeddings, biological databases, perturbation response, cell fitness, gene interaction, and natural-language explanations.

No quantitative axes or plotted experimental measurements are visible; the main content is a conceptual workflow describing CellHermes training tasks and downstream uses.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow and result figure for a biomedical AI model, CellWhisperer, linking transcriptome embeddings with natural-language text.

Panel a shows a model/training schematic: datasets from GEO metadata, ARCHS4 bulk RNA-seq, and single-cell annotations are converted into sample descriptions and conversations using LLMs; transcriptome and language encoders are trained into a shared 2048-dimensional multimodal embedding space. The application area shows free-text cell labeling and chat-based querying of cell samples.

Panel b shows a UMAP landscape labeled “An annotated landscape of human transcriptomes,” with many colored clusters representing 705,430 GEO transcriptomes in CellWhisperer embedding space.

Panel c shows a UMAP query result for the term “leukemia,” colored by a CellWhisperer score legend from negative blue to positive red. Red-enriched regions indicate transcriptomes matching the leukemia query.

Panel d shows three small histograms of GEO submission dates for selected queried sample groups, including activated myeloid differentiation in HSPCs, K562 erythroleukemia cells in culture, and obese adipose tissue immune/metabolic state.

Main visible finding: the model organizes large-scale human transcriptome data into a shared language-transcriptome embedding space that supports natural-language search, labeling, and biological sample exploration.

figure.caption: Figure 2: (a) Comparison of traditional single-cell analysis and CHATCELL. (b) Overview of CHATCELL.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model schematic for a single-cell analysis foundation model called **ChatCell**.

Panel **(a)** contrasts a **traditional paradigm** with **ChatCell**. It shows a pipeline from **cell mixture** to **single-cell RNA-seq**, producing a **single-cell gene expression matrix** with genes and cells, then converting expression into a **cell sentence** through **unified sequence generation**. The traditional side shows **cell expression embedding**, **foundation model pre-training**, and **task-specific fine-tuning** for multiple tasks. ChatCell is shown performing **single-cell analysis via chat**, taking instructions and returning task-specific solutions.

Panel **(b)** shows the ChatCell construction workflow. It includes **Instruction Construction**, where a task description, input cell sentence, and target output are assembled; **Vocabulary Adaptation**, combining an original vocabulary with domain knowledge to create an expertise vocabulary and initialize the model; and a **Unified Sequence Generation for Single-cell Analysis** module. Example tasks include **random cell generation**, **pseudo-cell generation**, **cell type annotation**, and **drug sensitivity prediction**. The visible examples show gene-list “cell sentences” and generated outputs such as a likely **spinous** cell type and **resistance/drug sensitivity** response. No quantitative axes or plots are present.

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a genomic AI model overview and token/task statistics.

Panel a is a biological diagram of sequence-related regulatory and molecular tasks around DNA/RNA/protein contexts. Labels include enhancer, lncRNA, DNA accessibility, promoter, UTR, exon, intron, splice sites, polyadenylation, RNA stability, RNA degradation, protein melting, protein fitness, DNA methylation, histones, and ChatNT as an AI assistant for biological sequences.

An example prompt asks for degradation rate of a human RNA sequence, and the output states the predicted degradation rate is 1.83.

Main visible finding: the figure presents ChatNT as a sequence-aware language model integrating DNA/RNA/protein biological tasks, with large-scale DNA and English token training data and an encoder-resampler-language-model architecture for biological sequence prediction.

figure.caption: Fig. 1 | Chroma is a generative model for proteins and protein complexes that combines structured diffusion for protein backbones with scalable molecular neural networks for backbone synthesis and all-atom design. a , A correlated diffusion process with chain and radius-of-gyration constraints gradually transforms protein structures into random collapsed polymers (right to left). The reverse process (left to right) can be expressed in terms of a time-dependent optimal denoiser ̂ t ( , ) θ t x x that maps noisy coordinates x t at time t to predicted denoised coordinates 0 x . b , We parameterize this in terms
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure for protein complex design using polymer diffusion.

Panel a shows a diffusion trajectory from a “collapsed polymer system” through noisy intermediate structures \(x_t\) to a “protein complex backbone” \(x_0\), followed by a “design network” producing an “all-atom complex.” Arrows label generation as reverse polymer diffusion and training as forward polymer diffusion.

Panel b illustrates denoising: a noisy structure \(x_t\) is processed by a random graph neural network with \(O(N)\) or \(O(N\log N)\) edges, producing confidence-weighted predicted inter-residue geometries, then an equivariant geometry solver outputs a predicted denoised structure \(\hat{x}_\theta(x_t,t)\).

Panel c is a probabilistic conditioning schematic showing a time-dependent prior \(\log[p_t(x)]\) plus time-dependent conditioners \(\log[p_\theta(y|x)]\) forming a time-dependent posterior \(\log[p_t(x|y)]\). Legend items include symmetry, substructure, shape, and semantics.

Main visible message: the method generates protein complex backbones by denoising collapsed/noisy polymer structures under optional structural or semantic conditioning, then converts the backbone to an all-atom protein complex.

figure.visible_model_interface: Random graph neural network and equivariant geometry solver
figure.rationale: Panel b directly shows the noisy coordinate input x_t and the immediate processing stack that consumes it before denoising, while excluding the unrelated conditioner/summary panels on the right.

figure.caption: Figure 1: BIOREASON Architecture. Schematic representation of our novel multimodal framework that integrates a DNA foundation model with a Large Language Model.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a genomics-language model system. It shows DNA sequences passed through a frozen Evo2-1B model, then a learnable linear projection aligning Evo2 embeddings to Qwen3 dimensions. These projected DNA embeddings are stacked with tokenized text embeddings from a BioReason chat template and Qwen3 tokenizer, using special DNA pad/start/end tokens and a Qwen3 embedding matrix. The combined embeddings feed into a Qwen3-4B model.

Visible labels include “Stacked DNA and Text Embeddings,” “Frozen Evo2-1B,” “Learnable Linear Projection,” “Qwen3 Tokenizer,” “Qwen3 Embedding Matrix,” “BioReason Chat Template,” “Question,” and “Response (with reasoning).” The example biomedical prompt concerns chromosome 12, pathway definition involving LRRK2, CYCS, APAF1, CASP9, and CASP3, and asks about the biological effect of an LRRK2 allele. The response panel gives chain-of-thought-style tags and concludes “Parkinson’s disease.”

Main visible point: the figure illustrates a multimodal architecture combining DNA sequence embeddings with biomedical text prompts to generate disease-related reasoning responses.

architectures.paper_title: Phenotype-Guided In Silico Molecular Generation Using Large Language Models

figure.caption: Figure  1.  Overview  of  the  GEMGen  framework.  a, Conceptual  illustration  of GEMGen. Given transcriptomic profiles describing transitions  between  healthy  and diseased  cellular  states,  GEMGen  generates  candidate  compounds  predicted  to induce the desired  phenotypic  change. b, End-to-end  workflow  of  GEMGen. Transcriptomic  changes  are  provided  as  text-based, rank-ordered  lists  of  up-  and down-regulated genes within a specific cellular context. GEMGen generates candidate compounds in SMILES format, which are optionally filtered by additional modules and ranked using the GEMGen scorer to prioritize candidates for experimental validation and downstream development. c , Model architecture and training strategy. GEMGen builds  on  a  scientific  foundation  model  (e.g.,  NatureLM)  adapted  from  a  generalpurpose  large  language  model  (e.g.,  GPT-5).  On  this  basis,  GEMGen  performs bioentity representation generation, followed by phenotype-guided compound generation  and  compound-phenotype  matching. d ,  Transformation  of  quantitative transcriptomic measurements into standardized, text-based features. Paired
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific schematic and results figure describing **GEMGen**, a generative model for compound design guided by cell-state gene expression phenotypes.

Panels include:
- **a:** Concept diagram showing compounds shifting a diseased cell-state landscape toward healthy.
- **b:** Workflow from an instruction prompt specifying cell type and up/down gene lists, through GEMGen generation, SMILES outputs, filtering, matching score, and experimental/clinical validation.
- **c:** Model architecture schematic: general-purpose language model adapted to scientific foundation model, with modules for bioentity representation generation, phenotype-guided compound generation, and compound-phenotype matching.
- **d:** Feature extraction workflow from transcriptomes to differentially expressed genes and ranked DEG lists, with labels for quantitative feature levels and robustness.
- **e:** Two density plots comparing cosine similarity distributions for random pairs vs duplications: DEG fold changes and DEG embeddings, with W-distance values shown.
- **f:** Training/evaluation setup listing L1000 compound-phenotype pairs, held-out compounds, single-cell chemical perturbations, genetic perturbation, and cell-state transition.

Main visible finding: the figure presents GEMGen as a phenotype-guided compound generation framework using DEG-based cell-state representations, with embedding-based DEG features appearing more robustly separated for duplicated profiles than raw fold-change features.

architectures.paper_title: GenNA: Conditional generation of nucleotide sequences guided by natural-language annotations

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a genomics foundation-model workflow and tokenizer/data analyses.

Figure type: workflow/model architecture plus plots and tokenization schematic.

Panels/labels:
- **a**: Pipeline diagram for “Multi-Modal Nucleotide Sequences” into a “GenNA Foundation Model,” described as a Qwen3 decoder-only transformer with 3.6B parameters, trained using causal language modeling. Inputs include NCBI RefSeq genomes, genomic DNA/RNA, natural language annotations, XML tags, and a cross-modal BPE tokenizer.
- **b**: Pie chart showing dataset composition: RNA dominates over genomic DNA.
- **c**: Overlaid length distribution histogram/density for genomic DNA and RNA sequences, x-axis “Length (characters),” y-axis “Density.”
- **d**: Two taxonomic composition pie charts with categories such as plant, invertebrate, vertebrate mammalian, vertebrate other, fungi, and protozoa.
- **e**: Schematic of multimodal input tokenization from a biological sequence containing tRNA and nucleotide text into BPE tokens and token IDs.
- **f**: Donut chart of tokenizer vocabulary composition, center label “Vocabulary 6000,” with legend by token type/k-mer length.
- **g**: Bar chart of k-mer length coverage, y-axis “Coverage (Count / 4^k),” showing highest coverage for shorter k-mers and decreasing coverage for longer k-mers.
- **h**: Scatter plot comparing character count and token count with a fitted line, showing near-linear correlation.

Main visible finding: the figure presents a cross-modal nucleotide-language tokenizer and GenNA foundation-model pretraining framework, with RNA-heavy training data, broad taxonomic coverage, a 6000-token BPE vocabulary dominated by longer nucleotide tokens, and an approximately linear relationship between character count and token count.
figure.visible_input_object: Panel a left-to-center workflow: the 'Multi-Modal Nucleotide Sequences' source box with NCBI RefSeq/GenBank files, genomic DNA & RNA, natural-language annotations, XML tags, and the 'Cross-Modal BPE Tokenizer', feeding via arrow into the 'GenNA Foundation Model' box.
figure.visible_model_interface: The crop includes the model-facing interface where the cross-modal BPE-tokenized inputs enter the GenNA decoder-only transformer in panel a.
figure.rationale: This is the smallest coherent crop that keeps the full source corpus box, the tokenizer step, the connecting arrow, and the immediate GenNA model box. It excludes the downstream 'Emergent Abilities & Generation' outputs and unrelated analysis panels.

routes.evidence_quote: We first evaluated unconditional generation under highly minimal conditions. In this setting, all explicit constraints were removed, and the model was provided only with a modality tag (Genomic DNA or RNA). It was then required to autoregressively generate the complete metadata fields, including species, gene name, and functional  annotation,  followed  by  the  corresponding  nucleotide  sequence.  For  generated mRNA sequences, we extracted the CDS regions and translated them into protein sequences, which were then aligned against existing databases using BLASTP 33 . We subsequently used Sentence-Transformers 34 to evaluate the semantic consistency between the model-generated functional annotations and the annotations associated with the top database hits. Sequence-logo analysis of these unconditionally generated mRNAs further recovered a Kozak-like translation-initiation context, which is a meaningful  local  sequence  grammar  (Supplementary Fig.  5).  The  results  showed  that  the  generated annotations remained well aligned with the corresponding generated sequences at the semantic level (Fig. 3b).

figure.caption: Figure 10: Schematic Illustration of the multimodal fine tuning using feature fusion via token concatenation with tokens derived from genomic as well as protein sequences and protein structures.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture diagram for a multimodal protein/RNA analysis model. The figure shows modality inputs including DNA/RNA-like sequence text, protein sequence text, and a protein structure image, passed through frozen modality encoders labeled `Evo2`, `ESM`, and `GAT`. Their embeddings are sent through trainable token projectors, concatenated with a tokenized natural-language question, and fed into a Llama model to generate an output answer.

Visible legend indicates ice cube icons as frozen parameters and flexed arm icons as trainable parameters. Labels include `Modality Inputs`, `Modality Encoders`, `Token Projectors`, `Token Concatenation`, `Llama`, `Tokenizer`, and `Output`.

The illustrated task asks whether a protein structure contains sites compatible with direct interaction with RNA-protein complexes. The visible output states that the protein structure reveals surface-exposed basic patches and conserved motifs often observed in RNA-binding proteins, supporting possible interaction.
figure.visible_input_object: Natural-language question text feeding the tokenizer
figure.visible_model_interface: Tokenized text inputs entering the token-concatenation stack immediately before Llama
figure.rationale: The current crop is defensible under the atlas rules because it visibly shows an actual model-input interface: the natural-language question and tokenizer path, plus the projected multimodal token stack immediately before Llama. It also includes the protein-structure-side embedded/projected representation entering that shared concatenation mechanism. A full model box or full upstream source object is not required when the serialized representation and immediate interface are visible. This shared architecture figure therefore supports the natural-language question route and the protein-structure virtual-token route.

figure.caption: Figure 2: (a) Comparison of traditional single-cell analysis and CHATCELL. (b) Overview of CHATCELL.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model schematic for a single-cell analysis foundation model called **ChatCell**.

Panel **(a)** contrasts a **traditional paradigm** with **ChatCell**. It shows a pipeline from **cell mixture** to **single-cell RNA-seq**, producing a **single-cell gene expression matrix** with genes and cells, then converting expression into a **cell sentence** through **unified sequence generation**. The traditional side shows **cell expression embedding**, **foundation model pre-training**, and **task-specific fine-tuning** for multiple tasks. architectures.paper_title: A Multi-Modal AI Copilot for Single-Cell Analysis with Instruction Following

figure.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of InstructCell. a, Summary of incorporated single-cell data. InstructCell incorporates 299,155 scRNA-seq samples from human and mouse origins, spanning multiple organs. CPCG denotes Conditional Pseudo-cell Generation , CTA denotes Cell Type Annotation , and DSP denotes Drug Sensitivity Prediction . b, Architecture of the multi-modal cell language model. The model processes both text and single-cell data via three primary components: a Q-Former to capture single-cell gene expression knowledge, a pre-trained LM as the backbone, and a cell reconstruction module for generating single-cell gene expression profiles. c, Construction of multi-modal single-cell instruction data. Complete instruction-response pairs are formed by combining required and optional attributes from text and single-cell modalities. d, Simulation of diverse communication styles. LLMs generate chat templates with varying traits (personality, motivation, and proficiency) to produce instructions that convey task-related information in different communication styles.

figure.caption: Figure 3 | Evidence of emergent zero-shot multimodal medical reasoning with Med-PaLM M. Large Med-PaLM M models exhibit zero-shot CoT reasoning capability in identifying and describing tuberculosis related findings in chest X-ray images. The model is prompted with task-specific instructions and a text-only exemplar (without the corresponding image) to generate a report describing findings in the given X-ray image. Model predictions from Med-PaLM M 84B and 562B are shown together with the annotations from an expert radiologist. Both models correctly localized the major TB related cavitory lesion in the right upper lobe. However, both models did not address the small cavitory lesion in left upper lobe (Med-PaLM M 562B was considered better than Med-PaLM M 64B in this example as it also alluded to the opacity in the right middle lobe and did not make the incorrect statement of left lung being clear). Notably, Med-PaLM M 12B failed to generate a coherent report, indicating the importance of scaling for zero-shot COT reasoning.

Quantity/task shown: Qualitative visual question answering evaluation for tuberculosis vs normal chest X-rays, comparing generated model explanations against radiology findings.

Main visible finding: The models identify a right upper-lobe cavitary lesion, but the annotations note missed findings, especially a small left upper-lobe cavitary lesion and a right middle/lower chest opacity likely related to TB.

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow and result panel for evaluating a language model on transcriptome embeddings. Left: question-answer pairs from a test set (`n=200`) combine a “transcriptome embedding” with a prompt question (“Describe this sample”) and ground-truth answer (“These are bronchial epithelial…”), passed into an LLM layer. The model outputs a prediction scored by perplexity.

Middle: scatter/strip plot of perplexity values, with x-axis “Perplexity lower is better” ranging roughly from 1.51 to 14.25 and y-axis categories 1–5. Legend distinguishes gray “Mismatched embeddings (n=30)” and purple “Matched embedding.” 

Right: horizontal quantile plot labeled “Perplexity quantiles for all 200 test cases,” showing inverted perplexity quantiles from 0 to 1.0. The visible result emphasizes that matched embeddings tend to have better/lower perplexity quantiles than mismatched embeddings.
figure.panel_label: Left workflow crop: transcriptome embedding + prepared question into adapter/LLM
figure.visible_input_object: Question-answer test-pair cards showing a purple 'transcriptome embedding' token, the question 'Describe this sample', and the answer bubble, with arrows feeding into the green CellWhisperer LLM adapter/LLM interface.
figure.visible_model_interface: The crop retains the embedding and question carriers plus their immediate ingress into the vertical green adapter/LLM block, which is the model-facing interface for the supported Mistral routes.
figure.rationale: The current crop is defensible because it contains the model-facing transcriptome embedding and question prompt, but it extends unnecessarily into perplexity-based evaluation. The same source figure contains a cleaner region: the left schematic alone. That region directly depicts the fine-tuning inputs for Mistral 7B, namely transcriptome-derived embeddings and prepared questions. It does not support the inference-only routes about cluster-averaged embeddings or hidden top-gene initiation.

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow and result figure for a biomedical AI model, CellWhisperer, linking transcriptome embeddings with natural-language text.

Panel a shows a model/training schematic: datasets from GEO metadata, ARCHS4 bulk RNA-seq, and single-cell annotations are converted into sample descriptions and conversations using LLMs; transcriptome and language encoders are trained into a shared 2048-dimensional multimodal embedding space. The application area shows free-text cell labeling and chat-based querying of cell samples.

Panel b shows a UMAP landscape labeled “An annotated landscape of human transcriptomes,” with many colored clusters representing 705,430 GEO transcriptomes in CellWhisperer embedding space.

Panel c shows a UMAP query result for the term “leukemia,” colored by a CellWhisperer score legend from negative blue to positive red. Red-enriched regions indicate transcriptomes matching the leukemia query.

Panel d shows three small histograms of GEO submission dates for selected queried sample groups, including activated myeloid differentiation in HSPCs, K562 erythroleukemia cells in culture, and obese adipose tissue immune/metabolic state.

Main visible finding: the model organizes large-scale human transcriptome data into a shared language-transcriptome embedding space that supports natural-language search, labeling, and biological sample exploration.

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a multimodal generative foundation model workflow and dataset/model architecture for H&E histopathology.

SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

The image is a multi-panel scientific figure labeled **a-d** about **EvenClock**, a clock-like spatial/text encoding scheme applied to a biological tissue/spatial transcriptomics example.

Panel **a** shows a schematic circular “EvenClock” layout. It has concentric rings labeled **sec**, **min**, and **hr**, with a center labeled **center cell**. The outer clock face is divided into sectors with clock-like positions labeled **12, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10**. A scale annotation indicates **“1× median_nn (sec ring radius)”**. To the right is an **“EvenClock text encoding”** box listing sector prefixes and top genes, examples including:
- **12-sec | TUBA1B, TMSB4X, STMN1**
- **12-min | GAPDH, ACTB, RPLP0**
- **2-sec | KRT1, COL1A1, COL3A1**
- **4-sec | MYH9, ACTA2, TAGLN**
- **6-hr | ALB, APOA1, HP**
- **8-min | CD3D, TRAC, CD8A**

A note states that each sector contributes top-N genes as a text prefix.

Panel **b** shows a colored tissue/spatial map labeled **Ground truth**, with cell or spot classes including **Spinal Cord, Brain, Cartilage Primordium, Lung, Liver, Heart, Dorsal Root Ganglion, Others**.

Panel **c** shows a similar tissue/spatial map labeled **OCellus prediction**, with many predicted anatomical or cell-type categories shown in a long legend.

Panel **d** shows a correctness map comparing predictions to ground truth, with legend entries **Correct**, **Others**, and **Wrong**. Most points appear marked correct, with scattered wrong predictions.

Overall, the figure presents a spatial neighborhood encoding method using clock-sector gene summaries, then compares model predictions against ground-truth biological tissue labels in an embryonic/anatomical spatial dataset.

routes.evidence_quote: 833,196 edges at confidence ≥ 0.70). Per -gene language-model embeddings from the frozen OCellus backbone serve as initial node features; binary indicators mark the knockout gene and baseline-expression genes; three graph-convolution layers propagate this signal through the network; and a multi-layer-perceptron head produces continuous log2 fold-change predictions. The graph neural network adds less than one million trainable parameters -three orders of magnitude smaller than the nine-billion-parameter backbone -and trains in hours on a single GPU. The full specification appears in Methods. The agent layer addresses a complementary limitation: even a powerful model is accessible only by writing custom code per task (loading h5ad, applying LoRA, decoding predictions, plotting results). OCellus-Agent organizes the full capability suite as a Coordinator -Expert -Verifier system over the same Qwen3.5-9B backbone. The Coordinator contains a trained Planner LoRA that decomposes natural-language queries into executable directed acyclic graphs of typed tool calls, a rule-based Router that dispatches each step to the appropriate expert role, and a threelayer Verifier that provides biological plausibility checks. Five expert roles -Data Loader, Annotator, Perturbation, Spatial, and Explainer -are implemented as dynamic LoRA swaps on the shared backbone, and a Tool Registry of fifteen registered tools is exposed via a Gradio web interface. Six interchangeable runtime configurations are loaded on demand through dynamic adapter swapping, so the entire agent occupies approximately twenty-two gigabytes of GPU memory on a single GPU rather than five separate model instances. For spatial transcriptomics, EvenClock discretizes two-dimensional coordinates into eighteen clockface sectors of text, allowing the same backbone to consume spatial context with no architectural modification; the spatial-encoding scheme is detailed in Results § 2.4.

routes.evidence_quote: Here we present OCellus, a single nine-billion-parameter language model that addresses all three limitations through three coordinated technical contributions on a shared Qwen3.5-9B backbone (Bai et al., 2025). The model is fine-tuned via LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) on twenty-two biological tasks spanning dissociated single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomics, including novel tasks such as cross-species cell-type annotation, developmental-stage prediction, and binary protein -protein interaction classification on the STRING database (Szklarczyk et al., 2023). First, EvenClock discretizes the continuous two-dimensional plane into a clockface of six directions and three distance rings, encoding each sector's neighboring cells as a gene -list prefix that the language model consumes as text with no architectural modification. Second, per-gene language-model embeddings extracted from the frozen OCellus backbone replace the Gene Ontology annotations that GEARS depends on, serving as node features for a plug-in graph neural network over the STRING v12 protein-interaction graph. Third, OCellus-Agent organizes the full capability suite as a Planner -Router -Verifier system that accepts natural-language biological queries and produces executable directed acyclic graphs of typed tool calls, with a three-layer Verifier providing biological plausibility checks. The unifying insight is that multitask language-model training yields a functional representation of every gene token that simultaneously drives spatial reasoning, perturbation generalization, and natural-language explanation; the full architecture is detailed in Results § 2.1. Empirically, OCellus attains Pearson correlation 0.945 on Replogle 2022 perturbation prediction, the OCellus encoder ranks first

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel workflow/model architecture figure labeled **A** and **B**. Panel **A** shows a cross-modal cell-text pretraining pipeline: scRNA-seq/cell omics data and cell description text are tokenized, passed through **Cell Encoder** and **Text Encoder**, aligned by **cross-modal similarity**, and trained with intra-modal cellular generative pretraining plus cross-modal cell-text pretraining. figure.caption: Figure 1: OmicsLM overview. Top: example questions from diverse omics datasets are formatted as multi-task conversations for OmicsLM, with each <omics> placeholder denoting a biological profile and gene symbols treated as explicit tokens. figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic for **OmicsLM**, a language model using explicit gene and omics tokenization. Multi-panel scientific schematic showing a genomic foundation model workflow and biological interpretation.

Panel A depicts the OmniNA model pipeline: pre-training on the NCBI nucleotide database using masked sequence annotation, data processing with prefix-style prompts, and large-scale transformer pre-training. It then shows fine-tuning on genomic tasks such as promoter prediction, mutation pathogenicity classification, and RNA off-target prediction. - **A:** Schematic of an “OmniHelix mutation effect score” for a genomic sequence around `chr7:1321843 A>G`, with formula comparing predicted mutation effects.

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel biomedical figure showing predicted mutation effects from an OmniNA model and comparisons with biological/clinical annotations.

Panels:
- **A**: Schematic definition of “OmniNA mutation effect score” for a single nucleotide variant, comparing log-likelihood of wild-type and mutant sequences.
- **B**: Two plots for **PAS** and **TIS** with x-axis “Predicted mutation effect,” left y-axis “Percentage,” right y-axis “Odd ratio.” Bars distinguish benign vs pathogenic proportions; red line shows odds ratio increasing with predicted mutation effect.
- **C**: Bar/line comparison of predicted vs experimental mutation effect across **gRNA sites**. Blue bars are predicted effects; red line is experimental effect.
- **D, G**: Bar charts for **BRCA1** and **CHD7**, comparing predicted mutation effect in domain vs non-domain regions, with p-value < 1e-5.
- **E, H**: Sequence-position heatmaps for **BRCA1** and **CHD7** amino acid sequences, annotated with protein domains such as zinc finger, BRCT1/BRCT2, chromo 1-2, ATP-binding, helicase C-terminal, SANT, and BRK. Color scale ranges from blue negative to red positive predicted mutation effect.
- **F, I**: Protein structure visualizations colored by predicted mutation effect, with labeled domains such as BRCT1, BRCT2, zinc finger, chromo 1-2, and ATP-binding.

Main visible finding: higher predicted mutation effect is associated with pathogenicity/enriched odds ratios and elevated effects in known functional protein domains, with domain-level mutation sensitivity patterns visible across BRCA1 and CHD7 sequence and structure.

figure.caption: Figure 6: Workflow for extracting biological embeddings from LLM-BFT. a : LLM-BFT generates profile texts for entities of interest (e.g., a specific gene). The gene profile text is encoded by OpenAI TEXT-EMBEDDING-ADA-002 (the same text encoder GenePT uses) to obtain gene embeddings, so that GenePT (GPT-4o + ada-002) and LLM-BFT (BFT-70B + ada-002) differ only in the LLM that produces the profile text. b : For a single-cell dataset, gene embeddings are weighted by gene expression values to generate cell embeddings.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model architecture schematic with two labeled panels, **a** and **b**. Panel **a** shows an LLM-based gene text embedding pipeline: a user prompt (“Tell me about gene.”) is processed by **LLM-BFT**, producing an LLM response with gene name/function/interaction text; texts for gene x through gene y are converted via **Text to embedding** into a **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix. Panel **b** shows a cell-by-gene expression matrix for **M cells** and **N genes** multiplied by the **gene embedding (N, 2048)** matrix to produce a **cell embedding (M, 2048)** matrix. Main visible message: gene-level text embeddings are derived from LLM responses and combined with gene expression data to generate cell embeddings.

figure.caption: Figure 2: CellPuzzles formulates cell type annotation as a batch-level reasoning task that integrates gene expression and contextual metadata, inspired by how experts annotate cells in practice.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/comparison schematic with two horizontal panels. The top panel shows a conventional human expert task: input cell clusters with representative marker genes, an expert assigns cell type labels, and output labels include Pulmonary Alveolar Type 2 cells, CD8+ Cytotoxic T Cells, Lung Pericyte, Alveolar Macrophages, and Plasma Cells. The bottom panel shows a “CellPuzzles Task”: given a batch of N cells with contextual metadata and candidate cell types, a model reasons jointly from top expressed genes and cluster/cell relations to determine optimal label assignment, producing labels such as CD4-positive alpha-beta T Cell, CD8-positive alpha-beta T Cell, Smooth Muscle Cell, Lung Macrophage, Non-classical Monocyte, Capillary Endothelial Cell, Plasma Cell, and Respiratory Basal Cell. No axes or quantitative plots are present; the main point is illustrating cell type annotation as a reasoning/assignment workflow.

figure.caption: Figure 2. Overview of OpticalDNA. (a) Render a 1D genomic sequence into a multi-page DNA document with bounding-box annotations. (b) Construct six OCR-style prompted genomic tasks. (c) Pretrain a visual encoder-document decoder under prompt supervision.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel model architecture and task schematic for DNA document understanding. Panels are labeled `(a) DNA document generation and visual encoding`, `(b) OCR-style prompt pretraining tasks`, and `(c) Trainable projection, fusion, and decoding`.

Panel `(a)` shows a 1D DNA sequence converted into a multi-page “DNA document” with spatial annotations, then patchified into `p x n x 16 x 16` patches and passed through a frozen visual encoder labeled SAM-Conv, CLIP, producing visual tokens. Panel `(b)` lists pretraining tasks T1-T6: Reading, Grounding, ROI, Completion, Retrieval, and Recognition, with prompts such as “Read the sequence,” “Locate each line in the sequence,” and “Classify document.” Panel `(c)` shows trainable components: projector, multi-page fusion, and document decoder, with prompt/response task instruction flow and loss `L_pt`.

No experimental plot or numeric biological result is shown; the figure mainly presents a workflow/model architecture for genomic reasoning primitives using visual document encoding of DNA sequences.
figure.visible_input_object: 1D DNA sequence rendered as a DNA document
figure.visible_model_interface: Patchify and frozen visual encoder input pipeline
figure.rationale: The current crop from Figure 2 validly shows the actual model-input mechanism shared by all listed routes: 1D DNA sequence rendered into DNA-document page images, patchified, encoded by the visual front-end, and passed through the shared OpticalDNA projection/fusion/decoder stack. Under the atlas rules, the prompt box is not mandatory when the crop clearly depicts the route-specific input object or representation supplied to the model, and this shared architecture can support multiple task variants that use the same depicted input mechanism.

architectures.paper_title: PROCYON: A multimodal foundation model for protein phenotypes.

figure.caption: Figure 4: PROCYON models domains, peptides, and small molecules beyond proteins. a) PROCYON predicts the small molecule binding domain on proteins, where the input is the description and molecular structure of a drug, and the output is a ranked list of domains on a target protein. In this example, PROCYON retrieves domains of MGAM given the drug miglitol and correctly prioritizes the binding domain for miglitol as the first among the MGAM's nine domains. Each domain is identified by the Pfam ID and the index of the first amino acid in the domain. b) PROCYON ranks the correct drug-binding domain (highlighted in orange) on respective target proteins highly. In Q06187, the green domain ( PF00017 281 ) denotes the PROCYON-predicted binding domain, but the orange domain ( PF07714 402 ) is the correct binding domain. PROCYON predicts the binding domain as top-ranked in 24 examples, second-ranked in 5 examples, and so on. c) PROCYON can be finetuned to predict protein-peptide binding. Left, PROCYON is first finetuned on naturally occurring protein-peptide complexes from the Protein Data Bank (PDB), then tested on an experimental dataset of synthetic peptides screened for binding to the ACE2 protein. Right, the predicted binding scores for binders versus non-binders. Two-sided Mann-Whitney U test. d) Leveraging PROCYON to perform indication-specific drug target retrieval. In this example, the input consists of a novel task definition, the description of indications (nicotine addiction or major depressive disorder), and the name and structure of bupropion. PROCYON ranks known targets (norepinephrine transporter (NET), dopamine transporter (DAT), and nicotinic acetylcholinergic receptor (AChR)) of bupropion among the top 40/18,174 human proteins. Shown are 95% confidence intervals derived by perturbing words in the input prompt. ** p -value < 0 . 001 ; two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure showing a protein-domain language/model workflow and biomedical prediction results.

Panel a: Workflow schematic for protein O43451 (MGAM), with a 3D protein structure, orange-labeled binding domain, input prompt text about Miglitol, domain decomposition, and a ProCyon output table ranking protein domains with scores.

Panel b: Three example protein structures for target drugs Apixaban, Sirolimus, and Ibrutinib, each with predicted domain-score tables. A bar chart below shows the number of binding-drug examples by predicted domain rank, with most examples at Rank 1.

Panel c: ProCyon-Bind training/testing schematic. Training uses natural protein-peptide complexes; testing uses synthetic ACE2 peptide binders and experimental binding data. A violin plot compares predicted binding scores for “Peptide ACE2 binder” vs “Peptide ACE2 non-binder,” with binders visibly higher and a reported p value of 1.04e-4.

Panel d: Disease-drug information retrieval examples for “Smoking cessation” and “Major depressive disorder,” with prompt/input/output boxes for Bupropion and structure images. Bottom plots compare rank/attention-style information contributions labeled disease and drug information, suggesting model emphasis differs across disease/drug text.

figure.rationale: This is the smallest clean crop that readably preserves the Figure 4a input route: the source protein/domain context, the transformation into domains, and the multimodal prompt with miglitol text and structure. routes.evidence_quote: Weconstructed a multimodal training corpus that integrated text-only, image-text, gene-text and imagegene-text data. These datasets were organized into a progressive three-stage curriculum designed to align histology, transcriptomics and biological language in a stable manner. To reduce catastrophic forgetting during training, the mixed data in the third stage also retained general text-only and general visionlanguage data, such as UltraChat and Flickr30k [49, 50]. In total, the corpus contained approximately 1.05 million images, 39.85 million text sentences and 151,182 tri-modal data pairs. Dataset composition and statistics are provided in Supplementary Table 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2. The module-level implementation and trainable components of this progressive curriculum are illustrated in Extended Data Fig. 1.
routes.section_heading: 3.4 Training corpus construction and progressive multimodal alignment

routes.route_label: gene expression profiles for transcriptome-to-language generation
routes.insertion_or_fusion_verbatim: autoregressive decoding
routes.evidence_quote: Transcriptome-to-language generation was evaluated on a held-out validation split of the gene-text paired dataset that was not used for model training. Each model was prompted with transcriptomic input to generate a biological description, which was compared with the corresponding transcriptome-grounded reference description using three complementary metrics. BLEU-4 measures local n-gram precision between generated and reference texts [30]. ROUGE-L evaluates sequence-level structural overlap based on the longest common subsequence [31]. BERTScore F1 computes contextual semantic similarity between generated and reference descriptions in embedding space [32].

routes.route_label: whole-slide H&E images for H&E-only case-level pathology workflow
routes.insertion_or_fusion_verbatim: projected into the hidden dimension of the language model and inserted into placeholders
routes.evidence_quote: We developed SciCore-Omics, a language-centred multimodal foundation model that unifies histology, spatial gene expression, and natural language within a shared token space (Fig. 1a,b). Specifically, the input histological images and gene expression profiles are processed by modality-specific encoders. Visual features are converted into a fixed number of vision virtual tokens through a visual encoder and a resampler module. Gene expression profiles are transformed into gene virtual tokens via a gene encoder, a Q-Former module, and a projection layer. The virtual tokens are then projected into the hidden dimension of the language model and inserted into placeholders, thereby forming a unified input embedding sequence. This sequence is further fed into the generative language backbone for autoregressive decoding. This design allows SciCore-Omics to treat histomorphology, molecular state, and user instruction as complementary contextual information in the same generative backbone, rather than as separate task-specific pipelines.

routes.insertion_or_fusion_verbatim: image-question-answer triples

routes.route_label: gene expression profiles for generative spatial domain recognition
routes.insertion_or_fusion_verbatim: autoregressive decoding
routes.evidence_quote: Another important task in spatial transcriptomics analysis is spatial domain identification [34-36]. We assessed SciCore-Omics in two settings. First, we examined whether the embeddings learned by the model encode spatial domain information by training a classification head on a frozen model to predict spatial domain labels. Second, we assessed whether the model can generate natural language descriptions containing spatial domain-related information. We defined the task as follows: for each spot, SciCoreOmics takes histological image patches and/or gene expression profiles as input to generate biological descriptions from which region labels, pathway labels, and marker genes are extracted (Fig. 4a). We conducted evaluations on a spatial transcriptomics dataset of the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) [37]. This dataset comprises 12 tissue sections with paired H&E images and spatial gene expression data generated by the 10x Genomics Visium platform, along with manual cortical layer annotations.
routes.section_heading: 1.4 SciCore-Omics improves spot-level spatial domain recognition

routes.route_label: histological image patches for embedding-based spatial domain recognition

For embedding-based evaluation, frozen model embeddings were extracted from image-only, gene-only or joint image-gene input and passed to a lightweight classification head. Performance was assessed using macro-F1 to account for class imbalance across spatial domains.
routes.section_heading: 3.9 Spatial domain, pathway and marker-gene evaluation

For each image, the model was given a dataset-specific closed set of candidate class names and instructed to return exactly one class label. No task-specific fine-tuning, parameter updates or in-context examples were used.
routes.section_heading: 1.5 SciCore-Omics supports zero-shot tissue-level histopathology classification

routes.route_label: H&E images for spatial gene expression prediction
routes.insertion_or_fusion_verbatim: top of SciCore-Omics visual embeddings
routes.evidence_quote: To evaluate whether histology-derived representations retained molecular information, we trained a lightweight regression head on top of SciCore-Omics visual embeddings to predict spot-level gene expression from H&E image patches. Experiments were conducted on the normal human heart spatial transcriptomics dataset comprising 39 sections. To avoid information leakage caused by spatial correlations between neighbouring spots within the same tissue section, we used section-level 10-fold crossvalidation. Specifically, the 39 sections were partitioned into 10 folds at the section level. In each fold, the model was trained only on spots from the training sections and tested on spots from the held-out section or sections. The prediction targets were the top 50 genes with the highest expression in the training set, and performance was evaluated on the held-out spots from the test sections. Before training and evaluation, all spots were subjected to quality-control filtering, retaining only spots with at least 500 detected genes.
routes.section_heading: 3.8 Spatial gene expression prediction from histology

routes.insertion_or_fusion_verbatim: case-level evidence summary
routes.evidence_quote: We next examined whether the model could extend this capability to a more clinically oriented caselevel reasoning setting. In this evaluation, only the whole-slide H&E images were used as the model input, while immunohistochemistry and pathology reports were withheld from the model and referenced solely for expert assessment (Fig. 6b). The inference workflow was designed to simulate a staged pathological review process. First, SciCore-Omics reviewed the low-magnification overview of the whole-slide image to identify tumour-rich regions and representative tumour-stroma structures. Second, representative tumour patches were selected from these regions for high-magnification assessment, with attention to interpretable morphological features, including tumour cell density, nuclear atypia, hyperchromasia, suspected mitotic activity, necrosis and stromal reaction. Finally, the model integrated evidence across multiple regions to generate a case-level interpretation of the proliferative status.

routes.evidence_quote: We developed SciCore-Omics, a language-centred multimodal foundation model that unifies histology, spatial gene expression, and natural language within a shared token space (Fig. 1a,b). Specifically, the input histological images and gene expression profiles are processed by modality-specific encoders. Visual features are converted into a fixed number of vision virtual tokens through a visual encoder and a resampler module. Gene expression profiles are transformed into gene virtual tokens via a gene encoder, a Q-Former module, and a projection layer. The virtual tokens are then projected into the hidden dimension of the language model and inserted into placeholders, thereby forming a unified input embedding sequence. This sequence is further fed into the generative language backbone for autoregressive decoding. This design allows SciCore-Omics to treat histomorphology, molecular state, and user instruction as complementary contextual information in the same generative backbone, rather than as separate task-specific pipelines.
