figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

The image is a multi-panel scientific figure with three labeled panels: `a. Dataset characterization`, `b. Model architecture`, and `c. Downstream analysis based on learned image embedding`.

Panel `a` summarizes dataset characterization. A circular chart shows microscopy/data categories including `BF`, `DIC`, `Conf`, `WF`, `SR`, `QPI`, `PC`, `Cell type (100+)`, `Perturbation (300+)`, and species labels including `Human`, `Mouse`, `Yeast`, and `Bacteria`. The center contains example microscopy cell images. A right-side hierarchy organizes data by `Granularity`, `Scale`, `Attribute`, and `Number`, mapping `Single-cell`, `Full-field`, `Subcellular`, `Cell-level`, and `Population` to attributes such as `Protein localization`, `Cell identity/state`, and `Perturbation response`. Counts are shown for `Pre-training` and `Evaluation`, including values such as `72,832`, `2,622,150`, `40,000`, `156,669`, `95,125`, and `117,628`.

Panel `b` shows a model architecture for single-cell image-text learning. Inputs include a generated `Caption` with keywords such as `Species`, `Source`, `Microscopy`, `Cell type`, and `Biological attribute`, plus a `Single-cell image`. The caption is passed through a `Tokenizer` into `Text tokens`. The image is passed through an `Image encoder` into `Image tokens`. A `Q-Former` module connects text/image tokens to image-text alignment, represented by a matrix comparing `Image feature` entries `I1 ... Im` with `Text feature` entries `T1 ... Tn`. A second shared-weight `Q-Former` receives masked image tokens, followed by an `Image decoder`, performing `Mask tokens reconstruction`.

Panel `c` illustrates downstream analysis using learned image embeddings. `Evaluation images` are input into `scMIR`, producing a learned image embedding matrix. The embeddings are used for `Cell classification`, `Morphological inference`, `Cell clustering`, and `Batch correction`, shown as schematic point clusters and transformed groupings.

Visible biological source objects include single-cell microscopy images and schematic cells. The figure describes transformations from microscopy images and captions into tokenized text/image representations, learned embeddings, reconstructed image tokens, and downstream biological analysis outputs.

routes.evidence_quote: For full-field microscopy images lacking provided cell boundary annotations, singlecell instances are obtained using an automated segmentation pipeline. Specifically, we apply  Cellpose  [59]  with  the  nuclear  channel  as  the  primary  segmentation  cue  to delineate individual cells. Following segmentation, each cell region is cropped from the original image, and zero padding is applied to produce square images. All images are subsequently processed by the pretrained image encoder and Q-Former to extract visual representations. The Q-Former outputs a fixed set of 32 query embeddings for each image,  each  with  a dimensionality  of  768.  To  obtain  a  compact  image-level representation, we compute the mean of the query embeddings, resulting in a single 768-dimensional  feature  vector  per  image.  For  multi-channel  microscopy  images, features are extracted independently from each channel using the same procedure. The resulting channel-specific feature vectors are then concatenated to form the final image representation, yielding a feature dimension of 𝑛 × 768 , where 𝑛 denotes the number of imaging channels.
routes.uncertainty: The paper notes that DIBaS and CM4AI do not undergo single-cell segmentation, so this route covers the full-field evaluation datasets that follow the shared preprocessing pipeline.

routes.evidence_quote: scMIR  is  a  vision-language  foundation  model  designed  to  learn  generalizable  and transferable representations from diverse single-cell light microscopy data (Fig. 1). The framework  consists  of three main  components:  large-scale dataset curation, a multimodal representation learning architecture, and downstream tasks evaluation. We first curated and harmonized publicly available microscopy datasets spanning multiple species, imaging modalities, cell types, and perturbations to capture broad biological and experimental diversity (Fig. 1a; dataset details are provided in the Supplementary information).  To  provide  consistent  biological  and  experimental  context,  structured textual  descriptions  were  constructed  using  controlled  keywords,  including  species, data  source,  microscopy  type,  cell  type,  and  related  annotations  (Fig.  1b).  scMIR integrates complementary learning objectives to capture both semantic and morphological  information. A  vision-language  alignment  module  associates  images with structured textual descriptions to enable cross-dataset semantic consistency, while an  image  reconstruction  module  preserves  fine-grained  morphological  features  to stabilize representation learning (Fig. 1b).

figure.caption: Figure 2 -Improved histology image synthesis from nuclear staining image. (a) Box plot of Pearson Correlation Coefficients (PCCs) between ground truth images and images generated by HistoPlexer, Pix2Pix-Turbo, and TissueCraftAI. n=462,549 image patches. Mean values are indicated. P-values were calculated using a one-sided t-test. (b) Box plot of Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) scores for the three methods using all test CODEX datasets. Lower values indicate better image quality. n=8 datasets. (c) Representative synthetic H&E images. For three different input DAPI images, the corresponding ground truth H&E images are displayed alongside the synthesized images generated by HistoPlexer, Pix2Pix-Turbo, and TissueCraftAI. The PCCs are shown for each synthesized image. Arrowheads indicate representative image imperfections compared to the ground truth.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel experiment result figure, labeled Fig. 2, comparing three image-translation methods: HistoPlexer, Pix2Pix-Turbo, and TissueCraftAI.

Panel a is a boxplot of Pearson Correlation Coefficient with y-axis from 0 to 1. TissueCraftAI shows the highest correlation, labeled around 0.915, compared with HistoPlexer around 0.825 and Pix2Pix-Turbo around 0.843. Significance brackets show p-values including p=0.024 and p=0.0076.

Panel b is a bar plot of FID Score. Lower is better visually implied by the comparison: TissueCraftAI has the lowest FID score, 138.4, compared with Pix2Pix-Turbo 209.0 and HistoPlexer 262.8. Significance brackets show p=0.00039 and p=0.00015.

Panel c shows qualitative microscopy/image synthesis examples in a grid. Columns are Input (DAPI), Ground Truth, HistoPlexer, Pix2Pix-Turbo, and TissueCraftAI. Rows show tissue image patches, with predicted histology-like outputs compared to ground truth. PCC values are annotated on generated images. The visible finding is that TissueCraftAI appears closest to ground truth and generally has higher PCC values than the other methods.

architectures.paper_title: TISSUENARRATOR: Generative Modeling of Spatial Transcriptomics with Large Language Models.

figure.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the TISSUENARRATOR framework. A. TISSUENARRATOR takes as input a tissue patch, encodes individual cells into cell sentences, and assembles a spatial sentence from neighboring cells. The spatial sentence can be interpreted by an LLM with biological prior knowledge and contextual understanding to predict gene expressions in a cell and to answer questions about tissues. Text output of the LLM can be further transformed into gene expression levels. B. TISSUENARRATOR supports four downstream tasks: cell generation, neighborhood perturbation, genetic perturbation, and conversational tissue querying. For cell generation tasks, model-generated cell sentences can be converted back into gene expression space.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Workflow/model schematic with two labeled panels, **A** and **B**. Panel A shows a tissue patch converted into “cell sentences” with ordered gene lists, then into a “spatial sentence” containing ordered cells with position, metadata, cell type, and gene list. An LLM with biological prior knowledge/contextual understanding is used for generative prediction, including cell prediction and text prediction, and quantitative prediction of gene expression values for genes such as G1, G2, G3. Panel B lists applications: cell generation, conversational tissue querying, genetic perturbation, and neighborhood perturbation. No numerical experimental data or axes are shown; the main content is a conceptual architecture/workflow for spatial tissue modeling with language-model-style representations.

architectures.paper_title: X-Cell: Scaling Causal Perturbation Prediction Across Diverse Cellular Contexts via Diffusion Language Models

figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure describing the **X-Cell** model and dataset. Figure type: schematic workflow, model architecture diagram, dataset summary, training procedure, UMAP visualization, and model-size bar chart.

Panels:
- **A:** Dataset/screen overview. Shows X-Atlas datasets **Pisces (25.6M)** and **Orion (8M)** across screens including **HCT116, HEK293T, HepG2, iPSC, Jurkat resting/active, and iPSC Multi-Diff**. Includes a stacked bar plot of cell counts in millions and a **UMAP2/UMAP1** embedding labeled “Cell x Screen,” colored by cell/screen type.
- **B:** X-Cell architecture workflow. Inputs from **X-Atlas/Pisces** feed gene perturbation information, prior knowledge sources such as **LLM/ESM2, STRING, DepMap, JUMP-cell painting, scGPT**, and gene-token/expression representations into a diffusion language-model architecture. The diagram highlights control encoding, perturbation conditioning, cross-attention, self-attention, and applications: **context generalization, perturbation prediction, and mechanism of action**.
- **C:** Training/inference schematic for **Gene X knockdown**, showing control input, intermediate prediction/remasking, and final predicted expression with control vs predicted color legend.
- **D:** Bar chart comparing model parameter counts in billions. X-Cell is labeled **55M 2026**, X-Cell-Ultra **4.9B 2026**, and other models include scGPT, Geneformer V2, STATE-SE, scFoundation, TranscriptFormer, and Tahoe-x1. A visible annotation indicates **92x** scaling from X-Cell to X-Cell-Ultra.

Main visible finding: the figure presents X-Cell as a large-scale single-cell perturbation foundation model trained on multi-screen atlas data, designed for perturbation prediction and biological generalization, with X-Cell-Ultra shown as substantially larger than X-Cell.

figure.caption: Fig. 5 X-Cell-Ultra generalizes to melanocyte progenitors and primary human T cells in a zero-shot manner. (A) Schematic shows pre-training of X-Cell-Ultra on X-Atlas/Pisces datasets, excluding the melanocyte progenitor population from the iPSC Multi-Diff screen. We evaluated X-Cell-Ultra in a zero-shot manner on the melanocyte progenitor population as well as primary human T cell datasets from Zhu et al. [57]. We used test-time adaptation to calibrate the models on these datasets using self-supervised objectives. (B) Test loss follows a power law with trainable parameters ( L ( N ) ∝ N -0 . 03 , R 2 = 0 . 97; Table A4). Five models (83M-3.1B) were trained for 20 epochs on the Replogle-Nadig dataset under identical hyperparameters. Circle size is proportional to parameter count; color indicates DE Pearson r . Line plots (right) show how X-Cell-Architecture (blue) and X-Cell-Ultra-Architecture (pink) compare with respect to collapse metrics δ -norm ratio (top) and Pearson correlation of differentially expressed genes (bottom) on test set. (C) Performance of the control mean baseline, perturbation mean baseline, STATE, X-Cell, and X-Cell-Ultra with respect to Pearson ∆ (left), differential expression direction match (middle), and mean absolute error (right). Histogram (top) shows the metrics within 1,341 perturbations and the barplots (bottom) show mean ± 95% C.I. (D) Boxplots show the distribution of Pearson ∆ (left), differential expression direction match (middle), and mean absolute error (right) for 291 perturbations in resting and stimulated (2 time points) primary human T cells for 2 different donors. (E) Heatmaps show the log 2 fold change in expression of APPL2 in D2 (left) and D3 (right) 48 hours post-stimulation as observed by the data and predicted by STATE, X-Cell, and X-Cell-Ultra.
figure.description:
SCIENTIFIC_FIGURE

Multi-panel scientific figure combining model/workflow schematic and quantitative benchmark plots for “X-Cell-Ultra.”

Panel A shows a workflow/model diagram: perturbation data from cell lines and iPSC-derived cell types, pre-training, and genome-scale zero-shot inference for primary human T cells, including “test-time adaptation” with frozen cross-attention/reduced learning rate.

Panel B shows model scaling dynamics: scatter/line plot of test loss versus trainable parameters for Replogle-Nadig, with Pearson r color scale, plus inset line plots comparing X-Cell and X-Cell-Ultra across epochs for Pearson correlation and differential expression Pearson correlation.

Panels C and D show benchmark results with histograms and bar/box plots for Pearson Δ, differential expression direction match, and MAE. Labels include melanocyte progenitor test perturbations, D2/D3 rest and stimulation contexts, and baselines such as control mean, perturbation mean, STATE, X-Cell, and X-Cell-Ultra.

Panel E shows clustered heatmaps of log fold-change values for APPL2 under D2 and D3 stimulation at 48 hours, comparing STATE, X-Cell, X-Cell-Ultra, and measured stimulation conditions.

Main visible finding: X-Cell-Ultra generally improves predictive performance, with higher Pearson/direction-match metrics and lower MAE than X-Cell or baseline methods, and shows improved scaling with larger trainable parameter counts.
